units.title: Exploration as data collection: epsilon, entropy and optimism
outcomes: Explain exploration as a data-collection choice and contrast directed optimism with undirected epsilon-greedy and entropy noise.
State the UCB selection rule and the regret criterion, and predict when epsilon-greedy suffers linear regret.
Name what an exploration bonus adds to a value target and what has to be tuned about it.
units.why: Every deep RL update eats data the current policy collected. If collection never visits the good regions, no update rule can recover them.

next.note: Turn the optimism bonus into count, pseudocount and prediction-error rewards.
Test exploration where rewards are sparse and comparisons are easy to rig.

study.locator: Lecture 9: bandit setting, regret as opportunity loss with counts and gaps, and the optimism-under-uncertainty versus Thompson-sampling approaches

study.title: Berkeley CS 285 Lecture 19: the exploration problem and optimistic deep RL
study.locator: Lecture 19, Part 1: the exploration problem with Montezuma's Revenge and the exploitation-versus-exploration definitions; Part 2: optimistic exploration in deep RL with the UCB exploration bonus and bonus-weight tuning

focus: Regret is cumulative opportunity loss written through gaps and visit counts, so minimizing regret and maximizing reward are the same objective stated two ways.
UCB picks \(\operatorname{argmax}_a Q_t(a) + c \sqrt{\ln t / N_t(a)}\): the second term is uncertainty, not noise, and it shrinks as \(N_t(a)\) grows.
Epsilon-greedy explores indiscriminately while optimism prefers actions that are nearly greedy or highly uncertain; that is why fixed \(\epsilon\) can keep paying linear regret.
In deep RL the bonus is added to the reward or value target, which makes the bonus weight a tuning parameter that changes the learned policy.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write regret as total opportunity loss and the UCB rule with all symbols defined. For \(Q = [0.9, 0.8]\), \(N = [100, 2]\), \(t = 102\) and \(c = 1\), compute UCB values 1.115 and 2.321 and pick arm 2 despite its lower mean, then explain why epsilon-greedy with fixed \(\epsilon > 0\) keeps linear regret.
traps: Reading UCB as mean plus noise. The bonus is a deterministic function of \(t\) and \(N_t(a)\); the randomness sits in the estimated means.
Assuming more exploration is always safer. A fixed bonus weight can drown the task reward, so the weight is part of the comparison, not a free setting.
Judging exploration by one training curve. Regret and coverage statements need counts and seeds, not a single run that happened to stumble onto reward.

selfTest.q: Two arms have means 0.9 and 0.8 with counts 100 and 2 after 102 pulls and c = 1. Which arm does UCB pick and why?
selfTest.a: Arm 2. Its UCB is about 2.321 against about 1.115 for arm 1, so uncertainty outweighs the lower mean.

selfTest.q: Why can epsilon-greedy with fixed epsilon have linear regret while UCB has sublinear regret?
selfTest.a: Fixed epsilon keeps pulling suboptimal arms a constant fraction of the time, so regret grows with t. UCB shrinks exploration of an arm as its count grows, so suboptimal pulls grow sublinearly.

selfTest.q: What does the bonus weight control when a UCB-style bonus is added to a deep RL target?
selfTest.a: How much the update prefers uncertain states over high-value states. Too large and the agent chases novelty instead of the task; too small and the bonus changes nothing.

selfTest.q: An agent scores highly once after random play. Does that show its exploration method works?
selfTest.a: No. One lucky trajectory shows reachability, not a method. Compare visit counts, success rates and regret across seeds under matched budgets.

units.stopWhen: You compute the UCB pick by hand, explain the linear-regret case for fixed epsilon, and state what a bonus weight changes in a deep RL target.

fit.note: CS234 Lectures 9 to 10 cover bandits, regret and UCB at explain depth and Berkeley Lecture 19 carries the deep RL bonus framing; no search needed.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: an epsilon-greedy versus UCB comparison on a small bandit and grid task with matched interaction budgets, reporting counts, gaps and regret across seeds.

units.title: Counts, pseudocounts, curiosity and intrinsic rewards versus shaping
outcomes: Explain counts, pseudocounts and prediction-error novelty, and when each bonus stays informative.
Derive the total-reward mix of extrinsic and intrinsic reward and show how beta changes the objective.
Implement a tabular count bonus and an RND-style predictor error on a small task without counting the bonus as task reward.
units.why: Sparse tasks give no gradient until the first success. Intrinsic rewards manufacture a signal from novelty, but the same signal can trap the agent in front of noise.

next.note: Measure intrinsic bonuses where rewards are sparse and shaping can mislead.
Plug exploration bonuses into off-policy actor-critic targets.

study.title: Pseudocounts from a density model
study.locator: arXiv:1606.01868v2 Sections 2 to 3: density model over states, learning-positive Definition 1, prediction gain and Theorem 1 relating pseudocounts to information gain, and the bonus built on the pseudocount form

study.title: Hands-on Modern RL 12.1: ICM and RND concepts
study.locator: Sections 1 to 3.1: sparse-reward motivation with total rewardmix, ICM state-prediction error with inverse and forward models, RND target and predictor with its intrinsic reward, and the ICM versus RND comparison (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Concepts only. The UCB line on this page drops the square root, so use the CS234 form with the root. Treat the 10-18 Montezuma probability and the Atari score claims as unverified author reports, not targets.

focus: Total reward is \(r^{total}_t = r^{ext}_t + \beta r^{int}_t\): with extrinsic 0, intrinsic 0.4 and \(\beta = 0.1\), the update sees 0.04, and changing \(\beta\) changes the optimum.
A usable bonus is computable from visited data and exhaustible: visited states must decay toward zero bonus or the agent farms novelty forever.
Pseudocounts generalize tabular counts through a density model, while RND skips densities and uses error against a frozen random target.
RND trains two value heads because extrinsic and intrinsic returns have different horizons: episodic task return versus non-episodic novelty return.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the total-reward mix, the ICM reward as half squared feature-prediction error, and the RND reward as squared predictor-minus-target error. Compute the 0.04 example above and explain the noisy-TV failure: ICM error never decays on unpredictable noise while the RND target has bounded complexity.
traps: Counting the bonus as task performance. Success rates and task returns must use extrinsic reward only; the bonus is training signal.
Trusting novelty from a representation without checking it. A bonus depends on features or densities, so a new encoder can flip which states look novel.
Treating episodic and non-episodic novelty as interchangeable. Non-episodic intrinsic return lets novelty leak across episode boundaries; RND Section 2.3 keeps two heads for exactly this reason.

selfTest.q: Extrinsic reward is 0, intrinsic reward is 0.4 and beta is 0.1. What update signal does the agent see, and what happens as beta grows?
selfTest.a: It sees 0.04. Larger beta pushes the policy toward novelty and away from the task optimum; the bonus weight is part of the objective.

selfTest.q: Why does ICM get stuck on a noisy TV while RND is more robust?
selfTest.a: ICM rewards forward-model error, which stays high on unpredictable noise. RND rewards error against a fixed finite-complexity target, so the error is bounded and decays with visits.

selfTest.q: Why does RND fit two value heads instead of one mixed return?
selfTest.a: Extrinsic return is episodic and intrinsic return is non-episodic with its own scale and horizon. One head would mix incompatible targets; two heads keep each bootstrap correct.

selfTest.q: A density model assigns high likelihood to a new state. What does its pseudocount say?
selfTest.a: High pseudocount, hence low bonus. The state looks familiar to the model whether or not a tabular count ever saw it, which is exactly the representation dependence to check.

units.stopWhen: You compute the mixed-reward example by hand, derive when each bonus decays, and keep bonus and task reward in separate columns of your results.

fit.note: Berkeley Lecture 19 plus the RND and pseudocount papers cover derivation depth and the hands-on page supplies concept examples; no search needed.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a tabular count bonus versus its pseudocount form on a small grid, plus an RND predictor-error bonus with extrinsic-only scoring and a noisy distractor cell.

units.title: Sparse, delayed and deceptive rewards, success coverage and unfair comparisons
outcomes: Distinguish sparse, delayed and deceptive rewards and predict which one misleads a shaped-reward fix.
Measure state-action visitation and success coverage with an explicit distance or threshold rule.
Spot unfair exploration comparisons that hide extra interactions, privileged state or tuned bonuses.
units.why: Hard tasks punish the wrong measurement. An agent can improve reward while never covering the goal, and a comparison can favor the method that secretly saw more.

next.note: Lock the matched budgets that make exploration comparisons fair.
Summarize sparse-task runs with robust aggregates instead of lucky seeds.

study.title: HER: sparse binary rewards and the shaped-reward failure
study.locator: arXiv:1707.01495v3 Sections 4.2 to 4.4 with Figures 3 to 5: DDPG with and without HER on pushing, sliding and pick-and-place over 5 seeds with the 7 cm and 20 cm success rule, and the failure of every shaped reward tried

study.title: CS234 Lecture 12: PAC, MBIE-EB and generalization
study.locator: Lecture 12: PAC framework for MDPs, MBIE-EB with its exploration bonus, and the generalization slides where raw counts fail when each state appears once and bonus terms are computed at visit time

focus: HER uses binary sparse reward \(r = -[\lvert g - s \rvert > \epsilon]\): 0 on success and -1 elsewhere, with success defined by an explicit distance such as 7 cm for pushing.
Deceptive means the shaped signal points away from the goal: HER Section 4.4 shows shaped rewards failing everywhere while sparse plus relabeling succeeds.
Coverage is measured over visited states and achieved goals, not over reward collected; a high-reward run can still cover almost nothing.
Fair comparisons match interactions, updates, information access and tuning: HER reports 5 seeds with standard-deviation bands and tunes its count-based baseline over a stated grid.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the HER binary reward and the pushing success rule, then sketch a visitation table for a small grid that separates success rate from state coverage. Explain in two sentences why the shaped rewards in HER Section 4.4 failed: they optimize distance while success is a threshold, and they penalize the touching behavior exploration needs.
traps: Replacing coverage with return. An agent can raise return by exploiting a nearby reward while the goal region stays unvisited.
Accepting a tuned baseline at face value. HER footnote 6 tunes its count baseline over alpha and beta grids; an untuned baseline comparison proves nothing.
Calling a task sparse when it is deceptive. Sparse needs more visits; deceptive needs a different signal, and extra visits to the wrong region make things worse.

selfTest.q: An agent doubles its episode return but visits the same 5 percent of states. Has exploration improved?
selfTest.a: Not shown. Return measures exploitation of visited regions; exploration needs visitation or success-coverage numbers over the state or goal space.

selfTest.q: Why did shaped distance rewards fail on the HER manipulation tasks while sparse binary rewards with HER succeeded?
selfTest.a: The shaped rewards optimize distance while success is a radius threshold, and they penalize imprecise touching, which teaches the agent not to touch the box. Sparse reward plus relabeling keeps the true objective and densifies signal honestly.

selfTest.q: Method A beats method B but used twice the environment steps and a tuned bonus. What do you demand before accepting the win?
selfTest.a: A rematch with matched steps, updates, information access and tuning budgets, plus per-run records and coverage numbers, not just mean return.

selfTest.q: Each state appears once in a large task. Why do raw counts stop helping?
selfTest.a: Every count stays near zero so every bonus looks the same. Novelty then needs generalization through densities, features or predictor error, with the representation dependence stated.

units.stopWhen: You report visitation and thresholded success separately from return, and you can reject an exploration win that hides extra steps, state or tuning.

fit.note: HER supplies sparse-task evidence with a success rule, hands-on supplies the bonus requirements, and CS234 Lecture 12 covers counts failure; no search needed.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: visitation and success-coverage logs on a sparse task, a shaped-versus-sparse comparison with the success rule fixed, and a fairness checklist covering steps, information and tuning.

units.title: Continuous actions, deterministic policy gradients, DDPG and TD3
outcomes: Derive the deterministic policy gradient as a chain of policy Jacobian and critic action-gradient.
Explain the TD3 target with twin-critic min, delayed actor updates and smoothed target actions.
Implement a DDPG-style update with replay and soft targets, then ablate the twin-critic min on a small continuous task.
units.why: Robot joints and steering take continuous values where DQN-style argmax is impossible. DDPG learns an approximate maximizer, and TD3 fixes the overestimation that otherwise feeds on itself.

next.note: Replace deterministic noise exploration with maximum-entropy stochastic policies.
Reuse off-policy continuous transitions across goals by relabeling.

study.title: Hands-on Modern RL 9.1: deterministic policy gradients and DDPG
study.locator: Sections The Fundamental Difficulty of Continuous Actions through DDPG: argmax by enumeration fails for continuous actions, the DPG chain-rule form, DDPG actor, critic, replay and soft target updates with tau = 0.005 and Gaussian exploration noise, and Three Weaknesses of DDPG (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Vocabulary and code sketch only. The displayed DDPG target drops the terminal mask; take the mask from the TD3 paper target and always multiply the bootstrap by not-terminated.

study.title: Hands-on Modern RL 9.2 TD3 part: twin critics, delay and smoothing
study.locator: Section Stability Improvements for DDPG: twin Q-networks with the min target, delayed actor and target updates every d = 2 steps, and target smoothing noise 0.2 clipped to 0.5 (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Use the paper for exact equations. The HalfCheetah curves and score claims on this page are author-reported; do not use them as targets.

study.title: TD3: clipped double Q, delayed updates and target smoothing
study.locator: arXiv:1802.09477v3 Sections 4 to 5: overestimation measurement with Figure 2, clipped double Q target Equation 10 as the min of two critics, delayed policy updates in Section 5.2 and target smoothing in Section 5.3; Section 6.1 ablation of the three parts

focus: Continuous argmax is the whole problem: DQN enumerates actions, so a seven-joint torque vector needs a learned maximizer instead.

The DPG form \(
abla_	heta J = \mathbb{E}[
abla_	heta \mu_	heta(s) 
abla_a Q(s, a)]\) needs states only, no action average, which is why DDPG can learn off-policy from a noisy behavior policy.
TD3 takes \(y = r + \gamma \min_i Q_i(s', \tilde{a})\) with \(\tilde{a}\) the smoothed target action: the min trades overestimation for underestimation, which the policy does not propagate.
Delay and smoothing serve the critic: the actor waits \(d = 2\) critic steps before following its gradients, and noise around the target action smooths sharp critic bumps.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the DPG chain rule from the stochastic form and write the TD3 target with all symbols. For \(r = 1.0\), \(\gamma = 0.99\), next-critic values 10.0 and 12.0 and no termination, compute 10.9 and state the delay and smoothing defaults.
traps: Dropping the terminal mask because a paper equation shows none. Paper targets abbreviate; your code multiplies the bootstrap by \((1 - d)\) with \(d\) the terminated flag, and truncation still bootstraps.
Reading the min as unbiased. Clipped double Q underestimates by design; underestimated actions are simply not followed, while overestimated ones would be chased.
Keeping Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise because the DDPG paper used it. Later work finds plain Gaussian noise works at least as well on common benchmarks; tune the scale instead of the process.

selfTest.q: Why can DQN not act in a continuous torque space without modification?
selfTest.a: Its decision rule needs argmax over actions. Enumeration works for two buttons and fails for infinitely many torque vectors, so it needs an approximate maximizer such as an actor or stochastic optimization.

selfTest.q: Next-critic values are 10 and 12 with reward 1 and gamma 0.99 and no termination. What is the TD3 target?
selfTest.a: 10.9. The min picks 10, giving 1 + 0.99 times 10.

selfTest.q: What breaks if the actor updates every critic step instead of with delay?
selfTest.a: The actor follows an inaccurate critic early, collects worse data, and the coupled error grows. Delay gives the critic more updates before its gradients steer the actor.

selfTest.q: A run reports high Q values but poor returns. Which TD3 mechanism addresses this and how do you confirm it?
selfTest.a: Clipped double Q. Compare single versus clipped-double runs on matched seeds and check whether the min lowers the value estimates while returns hold or improve.

units.title: Maximum-entropy RL, Soft Actor-Critic and temperature tuning
outcomes: Derive the maximum-entropy objective and its soft Bellman backup with the temperature weight.
Explain automatic temperature tuning as a dual update against a target entropy.
Implement or audit a compact SAC loop and compare it with TD3 under matched samples and tuning.
units.why: Deterministic actors explore only through added noise. SAC folds exploration into the objective with entropy, then tunes its own temperature instead of asking you to guess it.

next.note: Continuous control needs normalized actions and recorded wrappers before any ranking.
Compare SAC with PPO or TD3 under matched samples, compute and tuning.

study.locator: Sections Maximum-Entropy RL through Advantages of SAC: max-entropy objective, soft Bellman backup, Gaussian reparameterization, automatic temperature tuning with target entropy -|A|, and the DDPG/TD3/SAC table (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Vocabulary only. The temperature code sketch uses a confusing sign convention, so implement the dual update from the paper Section 5. Treat the table and curves as author reports.

study.title: Berkeley CS 285 HW3: SAC with entropy bonus and auto-tuning
study.locator: HW3 Section 3: SAC in src/agents/sac_agent.py with run_sac.py and experiments/sac configs; Section 3.3 entropy bonus; InvertedPendulum-v4 sanity returning close to 1000; Sections 3.4 to 3.5 fixed versus auto-tuned temperature

focus: The objective adds entropy: \(J = \mathbb{E}[\sum_t \gamma^t (r_t + \alpha H(\pi(\cdot \mid s_t)))]\), and \(\alpha \to 0\) recovers the standard return objective.
The soft backup replaces the hard max with a soft maximum over actions, which keeps several good actions probable instead of collapsing to one.
Auto-tuning solves a constrained problem: keep expected entropy above \(\bar{H}\) while maximizing return, with \(\alpha\) as the dual variable and \(\bar{H} = -\lvert A \rvert\) as default.
SAC wins on sample efficiency through replay and pays in tuning and stability: CS224R states the trade against PPO explicitly, including heavier Markov reliance.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the max-entropy objective, the soft backup, and the dual temperature update with target entropy. For a two-action uniform policy, entropy is \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\); with \(r = 1\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\) the augmented reward is 1.0693.
traps: Citing the first SAC paper for temperature tuning. The 2018 version uses fixed temperature; automatic tuning arrives in the 2019 applications version Section 5, which the pool points at.
Reading entropy as pure exploration noise. It regularizes the objective and smooths Q, so removing it changes the optimum, not just the samples.
Expecting auto-tuning to beat a tuned fixed temperature. HW3 notes the HalfCheetah default is already well tuned, so the win is robustness on new tasks, not a higher score there.

selfTest.q: What does the temperature alpha weight, and what happens at alpha near zero?
selfTest.a: The entropy term against reward. Near zero the objective recovers standard expected return and the policy can collapse to a single action.

selfTest.q: A two-action policy is uniform with reward 1 and alpha 0.1. What augmented reward does SAC optimize?
selfTest.a: About 1.0693, since entropy ln 2 is about 0.693 and 1 + 0.1 times 0.693 is 1.0693.

selfTest.q: Entropy keeps falling below target during training. Which way should alpha move and why?
selfTest.a: Up. Alpha is the dual variable on the entropy constraint, so low entropy raises alpha to price randomness back in.

selfTest.q: SAC beats PPO on samples but PPO is picked for a new robot task. What justifies that choice?
selfTest.a: Stability and tuning cost. SAC is more sample efficient but harder to tune and leans harder on the Markov assumption; PPO trades samples for plug-and-play stability.

units.title: Goal-conditioned policies, hindsight relabeling and partial observability
outcomes: Explain goal-conditioned policies and hindsight relabeling with recomputed rewards.
Compare final, future, episode and random relabeling strategies and state when each wins.
Describe partial observability and the history-as-state remedy, and state what stays at vocabulary depth here.
units.why: Sparse goal tasks give almost no successes to learn from. Relabeling turns every failure into a success for the goal actually reached, which densifies reward without inventing signal.

next.note: Contrast relabeled online data with fixed offline datasets and coverage gaps.
Record goal, wrapper and version identity so relabeled runs stay comparable.

study.title: SB3 tips: Markov assumption and history remedy
study.locator: Tips and Tricks when creating a custom environment: do not break the Markov assumption and supply observation history under delay, plus separate timeout truncation handling (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Vocabulary only for partial observability. Recurrent policies stay at vocabulary depth in this section; no pool homework trains one.

focus: A relabeled transition is \((s \Vert g', a, r', s' \Vert g')\) with \(r' = r(s, a, g')\): the goal is substituted and the reward is recomputed, never copied from the original goal.
Relabeling needs an off-policy algorithm because replayed data comes from a different goal and an older policy than the current one.
Future relabeling with \(k = 4\) or \(k = 8\) goals per transition wins because goals just after the transition stay reachable and informative; random goals from anywhere usually do not.
Partial observability means the observation alone is not Markov; stacking history restores information but does not guarantee a Markov state, and recurrent policies are only vocabulary here.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write one relabeled transition with its recomputed binary reward for a two-step episode. State the four HER strategies and why future with k = 4 wins, plus the dynamics-consistency condition for relabeling across goals.
traps: Copying the original reward onto the relabeled goal. The reward function runs again under the substituted goal; a failure for the commanded goal is often a success worth 0 for the achieved one.
Relabeling across tasks with different dynamics. CS224R allows relabeling only where dynamics stay consistent; otherwise the stored transition describes an impossible world.
Claiming recurrent-policy skill from this section. The pool has no recurrent homework, so history stacking is a baseline and recurrence stays vocabulary.

selfTest.q: An episode aimed at goal g ends at state sT. What exactly is stored for a relabeled goal g' = sT?
selfTest.a: Transitions (s||g', a, r', s'||g') with r' recomputed as r(s, a, g'). The achieved goal earns 0 under the binary reward while the original goal keeps -1.

selfTest.q: Why does HER require an off-policy algorithm?
selfTest.a: Relabeled transitions come from a different goal and an older behavior policy than the current target policy, so an on-policy update would use the wrong distribution.

selfTest.q: Which relabeling strategy wins in HER ablations and why?
selfTest.a: Future with k = 4 or 8. Goals observed just after the transition are reachable and informative; final is good but weaker, episode is mixed, and random is worst.

selfTest.q: Observations arrive with a one-step delay. What is the first fix and what does it not guarantee?
selfTest.a: Supply observation history as input. It restores information but does not guarantee a Markov state or match a learned recurrent policy.

units.stopWhen: You write a correct relabeled transition with its recomputed reward, rank the four strategies from evidence, and state the history remedy with its limits.

fit.note: Goal relabeling is covered by CS224R Lecture 12 and HER, but partial observability has no pool locator under the use notes; SB3 custom-env history guidance fills that vocabulary gap.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a goal relabeling test on a small sparse-reward task that checks substituted goals with recomputed rewards across final and future strategies, plus a history-stacking baseline on a delayed-observation variant.

study.locator: Tips and Tricks when creating a custom environment: normalize observations and rescale continuous actions to [-1, 1], verify with check_env, handle timeout truncation separately, and the evaluation warning that wrappers change measured rewards and lengths (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Step returns five values: \(terminated\) ends the MDP and \(truncated\) stops it from outside, and only truncation bootstraps the next value.

Vector envs default to NEXT_STEP autoreset: the done step returns the true final transition, then the next step ignores its action and returns the reset observation with reward 0 and both flags false.
Gaussian policies start centered at 0 with unit width, so unnormalized action spaces harm learning silently; rescale to \([-1, 1]\) inside the recorded wrapper.
Every wrapper that touches reward, length or observation is part of the env identity: TimeLimit length, action repeat, normalization stats and reward transforms all get versioned.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the five-tuple step contract and the bootstrap rule for each end flag. For a 2-env vector run with max steps 5, state which step returns the true final transition and why the following autoreset step with reward 0 must never be stored as a transition.
traps: Reading final_observation or final_info on Gymnasium 1.x. Those keys exist only in same-step mode; the default next-step mode removed them, and CleanRL-era code that needs them raises KeyError at truncation.
Storing the autoreset step as experience. Its action was ignored and its reward is 0 by construction, so training on it teaches a fake transition.
Comparing across different wrapper stacks. A normalized versus raw observation run or a different TimeLimit length is a different environment, not a better algorithm.

selfTest.q: An episode ends at the TimeLimit with no terminal state. Do you bootstrap the value target?
selfTest.a: Yes. Truncation stops the MDP externally, so the value beyond the boundary still matters. Only true termination cuts the bootstrap.

selfTest.q: A vector step returns done flags true and the next step returns reward 0 with flags false. What happened?
selfTest.a: NEXT_STEP autoreset. The done step carried the true final transition; the next step reset the sub-env and ignored its action. Do not store the reset step as a transition.

selfTest.q: Old code reads infos final_observation on Gymnasium 1.4 and crashes at truncation. Why?
selfTest.a: That key exists only in same-step autoreset mode. The installed default is next-step mode, where the final observation arrives on the done step itself and the info keys are gone.

selfTest.q: Two SAC runs differ only in that one normalizes observations. Can you rank the algorithms from them?
selfTest.a: No. Normalization changes the task interface, so the runs measure different setups. Match the full wrapper stack first, then compare.

units.stopWhen: Your manifest rebuilds an env bit-identically, your bootstrap test passes for both end flags, and no comparison you report mixes wrapper stacks.

study.title: Precipice paper: why point estimates fail
study.locator: arXiv:2108.13264v4 Sections 1 to 3: unreliable point estimates, the Atari 100k case study with median uncertainty even at 50 runs, and the call for interval estimates over point scores

focus: Evaluate on a separate test env, never on training rollouts: training actions carry exploration noise, so training return understates or misstates the policy.
Deterministic eval usually scores higher for stochastic policies but it is a different policy; report which mode produced each number.
Seeds vary initialization and sampling, episodes vary trajectory noise under one policy, and environments vary the task itself: resampling the wrong unit answers the wrong question.
Training curves proxy progress but underestimate the agent; periodic clean evaluation with \(n\) between 5 and 20 episodes is the estimate to trust.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the evaluation protocol: separate test env, EvalCallback cadence, deterministic flag stated, several seeds, wrapper-matched. Explain in two sentences why a median over 3 runs can still mislead, using the precipice case study.
traps: Evaluating without a Monitor wrapper and quoting the numbers. SB3 warns unwrapped eval envs misreport lengths and rewards; the warning is the lesson.
Mixing stochastic and deterministic eval numbers across methods. Pick one mode per comparison or report both with labels.
Treating episodes as seeds. More episodes shrink trajectory noise for one policy; only more seeds show sensitivity to initialization and sampling luck.

selfTest.q: Why must evaluation use a separate test env instead of training rollouts?
selfTest.a: Training rollouts use exploration noise and evolving behavior, so their returns do not estimate any fixed policy. A separate env with a fixed eval policy measures what the agent actually learned.

selfTest.q: Deterministic eval scores higher than stochastic eval on the same weights. Which number do you report?
selfTest.a: The one matching your claim, labeled. Deterministic mode is a different policy; report the mode with the number and keep it fixed across methods.

selfTest.q: Three seeds give means 100, 200 and 900. What is wrong with reporting the mean?
selfTest.a: One lucky run dominates and the spread is hidden. Report per-run records with a robust aggregate and interval, and keep the outlier in the data.

selfTest.q: What changes when you add episodes versus adding seeds?
selfTest.a: Episodes reduce trajectory noise for fixed policies; seeds reveal sensitivity to initialization and sampling. They are different uncertainty units.

units.stopWhen: Your eval harness runs a labeled deterministic protocol on a separate env across seeds, and you can explain what each uncertainty unit varies.

outcomes: Compute the interquartile mean as a 25 percent trimmed mean across all runs.
Read and build performance profiles as score distributions over thresholds.

units.why: A few lucky runs can make any method look best. IQM plus profiles plus stratified intervals show the whole distribution instead of the luckiest point.

study.title: Precipice paper: stratified bootstrap, profiles and IQM
study.locator: arXiv:2108.13264v4 Section 4.1: stratified bootstrap resampling runs independently per task; Section 4.2: performance profiles as run-score distributions over thresholds with bootstrap bands; Section 4.3: IQM as the 25 percent trimmed mean with Figures 6 to 7

study.title: rliable: aggregate_iqm, interval estimates and profiles
study.locator: rliable/metrics.py: aggregate_iqm with trim_mean proportiontocut 0.25 and probability_of_improvement; rliable/library.py: get_interval_estimates returning point estimates then interval arrays of shape (2, ...) with row 0 lower and row 1 upper, and create_performance_profile over tau_list with use_score_distribution

focus: IQM discards the bottom and top 25 percent of all runs and means the rest: for scores 0 to 7 it is 3.5, the mean of 2, 3, 4 and 5.
A profile value at \(\tau\) is the fraction of runs scoring above \(\tau\); higher curves are better and crossing curves mean the ranking depends on the threshold.
Stratified bootstrap resamples runs independently within each task, which respects the runs-times-tasks structure instead of pooling everything.
Report the aggregate with its interval and keep the per-run data: the interval is the result, not decoration on a point estimate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute IQM of 0 to 7 as 3.5 and a profile value for a tiny score set at one threshold. Write the rliable call as point, interval = get_interval_estimates with a seed, and state the CI row layout.
traps: Unpacking the interval call backwards. It returns point estimates first and intervals second; the docstring example also names a wrong dtile function, so call metrics.aggregate_iqm exactly.
Reading CI rows swapped. Row 0 is the lower bound and row 1 the upper; swapped rows print nonsense like (0.449, 0.445).
Averaging task means before profiling. Score distributions across all runs carry less uncertainty than average-score distributions; the library defaults to score distributions for this reason.

selfTest.q: Scores 0 to 7 across runs. What is the IQM?
selfTest.a: 3.5. Drop the bottom two and top two values 0, 1, 6, 7 and mean the remaining 2, 3, 4, 5.

selfTest.q: A profile shows 0.1 for A and 0.5 for B at threshold 0.6. What does that say?
selfTest.a: Half of B runs beat 0.6 against a tenth of A runs. It compares full distributions at that threshold, not just centers.

selfTest.q: Why resample runs independently per task instead of pooling all scores?
selfTest.a: Tasks have different scales and difficulties. Stratification keeps each task represented and stops an easy task from dominating the interval.

selfTest.q: Two curves cross in a performance profile. Which method is better?
selfTest.a: Neither uniformly. Each wins on some threshold range; report IQM with intervals plus the profiles instead of picking one threshold.
